Healer
HEEL-ur
n. (one who cures or binds up; in Isaiah, an office a man refuses to take)
Old English haelan, to make whole — the same root as whole, hale and holy. To heal is to make entire. In Isaiah 3 it renders Hebrew chabash, to bind up, as a bandage binds a wound.

Biblical Definition

The word appears in a strange place. Isaiah is describing the collapse of Judah, when the state is so broken that men will grab a brother in the street and say, thou hast clothing, be thou our ruler — and the brother will swear in that day, I will not be an healer; for in my house is neither bread nor clothing: make me not a ruler of the people. The Hebrew is chabash, to bandage. To rule, in Isaiah's vocabulary, is to bind up wounds; and the mark of a society under judgment is that no one will take the bandage. Against that refusal Scripture sets the LORD who does not refuse. I am the LORD that healeth thee is given at Marah, where bitter water was made sweet by a tree cast into it, and it is given as a name. He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds — the same binding verb, now in God's hands, and applied to an injury no physician can reach. Christ took the title as his own work when he quoted the proverb Physician, heal thyself back to Nazareth, and he had opened his ministry there by reading Isaiah's commission to bind up the brokenhearted. The men of Isaiah 3 would not be healers. The Son of God came to be one, and was wounded doing it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one that cures or heals; that which makes whole or restores to soundness.

expand to see more

HEALER, n. One that cures or heals.

HEAL, v.t. To cure of a disease or wound and restore to soundness; to make whole.

HEAL, v.t. To reconcile, as a breach or difference; to make whole; to free from evil.

BIND, v.t. To tie together, or confine with a cord or bandage.

PHYSICIAN, n. A person skilled in the art of healing; one whose profession is to prescribe remedies for diseases.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 3:7 — "In that day shall he swear, saying, I will not be an healer; for in my house is neither bread nor clothing: make me not a ruler of the people."

Exodus 15:26 — "And said, If thou wilt diligently hearken to the voice of the LORD thy God, and wilt do that which is right in his sight, and wilt give ear to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will put none of these diseases upon thee, which I have brought upon the Egyptians: for I am the LORD that healeth thee."

Psalm 147:3 — "He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds."

Luke 4:23 — "And he said unto them, Ye will surely say unto me this proverb, Physician, heal thyself: whatsoever we have heard done in Capernaum, do also here in thy country."

Modern Corruption

Healing is claimed as a right the believer may command and marketed by men who bill for it; Scripture presents it as the free act of a sovereign physician who sometimes says, my grace is sufficient for thee.

expand to see more

The faith-healing trade takes a real promise and turns it into a contract: God has already purchased your healing, so claim it, and if nothing happens the failure is yours. The pastoral cruelty of this is hard to overstate — it lays the weight of an unhealed body on the sick person's faith. Scripture refuses the arrangement outright. Paul left Trophimus at Miletum sick. Timothy was told to take a little wine for his stomach's sake and his often infirmities. Paul himself besought the Lord thrice about the thorn and was answered not with healing but with my grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. No apostle ever told a sick believer that his sickness was evidence against him.

The opposite error quietly stops asking. Because the abuse is so visible, sober churches can drift into a practical cessationism of prayer — not denying that God heals, simply never expecting it. James gives plain instruction against that drift: is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. The God who is named the LORD that healeth thee has not retired. He heals whom he will, when he will, and finally and completely on a morning when there shall be no more pain, for the former things are passed away.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rapha (H7495), to heal or mend; chabash (H2280), to bind up as with a bandage; Greek iaomai (G2390), to cure; iatros (G2395), a physician.

expand to see more

Hebrew rapha (H7495) — to heal, to repair; behind the covenant name Jehovah-rophe, the LORD that healeth thee.

Hebrew chabash (H2280) — to bind up, to bandage; rendered healer in Isaiah 3 and bindeth up in Psalm 147.

Greek iaomai (G2390) — to cure, to heal; used of bodies and of souls, by whose stripes ye were healed.

Greek therapeuo (G2323) — to attend, to treat, to heal; the root behind therapy.

Greek iatros (G2395) — a physician; they that are whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.

Usage

"“I will not be an healer” — the office refused in a collapsing nation."

"“I am the LORD that healeth thee” — given at Marah as a name."

"“He healeth the broken in heart” — an injury beyond any physician."
